summary: Defines the operations of SNMPv2 in terms of how messages are sent and received. It covers requests for reading and changing management data and the replies and notifications that come back. It was replaced by RFC 3416.

eli5.summary: This is the list of questions and answers a network manager can use with a device: please tell me this fact, please change that setting, and I am telling you something just happened.

questions: how does snmp get and set work
what is the difference between getnext and getbulk
what is a variable binding in snmp
subtitle: The eight message types SNMPv2 managers and agents use to read, change and report management data.

tldr.problem: A management station needs a precise set of operations for reading and changing data on many network devices, and for hearing about problems, over an unreliable datagram service.
tldr.mechanism: SNMPv2 defines a set of protocol data units (Get, GetNext, GetBulk, Set, Response, Inform, Trap and Report) and exact rules for how a receiver builds the reply to each one.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1905 obsoletes RFC 1448 and was itself obsoleted by RFC 3416, so it is no longer the current definition of these operations.

facts.label: PDU types
facts.value: Get, GetNext, GetBulk, Response, Set, Inform, Trap, Report

today: RFC 1905 is a Draft Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 3416, which now defines these protocol operations. It had itself obsoleted RFC 1448.

sections.title: What the Protocol Operations Cover
sections.content:
An SNMP management system has agents (processing entities on devices that can reach management information), at least one management station, and a management protocol that carries information between them. The information is a collection of managed objects held in a virtual store called the Management Information Base (MIB).

Each SNMPv2 message is a message wrapper around a Protocol Data Unit (PDU). The wrapper is defined by an administrative framework that handles authentication and authorization. RFC 1905 defines only what happens when PDUs are sent and received. For the original framework it uses the name SNMPv1, and for the current one SNMPv2.
sections.eli5: A message is like an envelope with a letter inside. This document is about the letters: what each kind says and how to answer it.

sections.title: Roles, Sizes and Transport
sections.content:
An SNMPv2 entity can act in a manager role, an agent role, or both. It can also act as a proxy agent, which looks like an agent but answers requests by acting as a manager toward a remote entity. The protocol offers three kinds of access: a manager asks an agent and gets a response, a manager asks another manager and gets a response, and an agent sends an unconfirmed trap to a manager.

Every request normally gets a response. Whether to retransmit an unanswered request is up to the application, which must act responsibly about how often and how long it retries. A message may be no larger than the smaller of what the sender can generate and what the receiver can accept.

Only an unreliable datagram service is needed, with each message contained entirely in one transport datagram. The preferred mapping is the User Datagram Protocol, and other mappings are specified elsewhere. The memo says security issues are not discussed in it.
sections.eli5: Usually one side asks and the other answers, like a teacher and a student. Each message has to fit in a single envelope, and the sender must not send an envelope bigger than the receiver can open.

sections.title: PDU Types and Fields
sections.content:
The definitions are written in ASN.1. Most PDUs share one layout of four fields: request-id, error-status, error-index and variable-bindings. A variable binding pairs the name of a variable with its value. In a retrieval request the value slot holds unSpecified, and in a response it may hold one of the exceptions noSuchObject, noSuchInstance or endOfMibView.

The request-id in a Response-PDU copies the request's, so a manager can match replies to outstanding requests and spot duplicates. A non-zero error-status means something prevented processing, and error-index then names which binding (counting from one) caused it. The error-status values run from noError(0) to inconsistentName(18).

The GetBulkRequest-PDU replaces error-status and error-index with non-repeaters and max-repetitions. Object identifiers are limited to 128 sub-identifiers, each with a maximum value of 2**32-1.
sections.eli5: Each message is a form with a ticket number, an error box and a list of questions with blanks for answers. The ticket number lets the asker match each answer to the right question.

sections.title: Reading Data: Get, GetNext and GetBulk
sections.content:
For a GetRequest, the agent fills in each named variable's value. If the name matches no object it sets noSuchObject, and if the object exists but the instance does not it sets noSuchInstance. For a GetNextRequest, the agent returns the first variable that comes after the given name in lexicographic order, which lets a manager walk through a MIB or a table. If there is none it returns endOfMibView.

A GetBulkRequest does many GetNext steps in one exchange. The first N bindings (limited by non-repeaters) get one successor each, and each of the remaining R bindings gets up to M successors, where M is max-repetitions. The response holds at most N + (M * R) bindings, and may hold fewer if the message would be too large or the agent runs out of time. The RFC's example shows the same table traversal done with fewer exchanges than GetNext.

If a response would be too big, the agent sends a tooBig response with an empty binding list. If even that is too big, the snmpSilentDrops counter is incremented and the message is discarded. Because large messages can be fragmented, the RFC says GetBulk senders must keep max-repetitions small under network stress.
sections.eli5: Get is asking for one page of a book. GetNext is asking for the next page. GetBulk is asking for the next several pages at once, so you do not have to keep asking.

sections.title: Changing Data: SetRequest
sections.content:
A SetRequest is processed as a conceptual two-phase operation. In the first phase every variable binding is checked in order, and the first failure stops processing and is reported with a specific error such as noAccess, notWritable, wrongType, wrongLength, wrongValue, noCreation, inconsistentName, inconsistentValue or resourceUnavailable. Anything else gives genErr.

If all checks pass, the second phase assigns every value as if simultaneously. If an assignment still fails, all the others are undone and the reply says commitFailed. Only if the undo is impossible does it say undoFailed. The RFC strongly encourages implementations to avoid both codes and says they are not a license to take the easy way out. If the same variable appears twice with different values, which one wins is implementation-specific.
sections.eli5: Changing settings is done like a careful teacher: first check every change on the list is allowed, then make them all together. If one fails, put everything back.

sections.title: Traps, Informs and Responses
sections.content:
An agent sends an SNMPv2-Trap-PDU when an exceptional situation occurs, and no reply comes back. Where it goes is implementation-dependent. A manager sends an InformRequest-PDU to tell another manager about information in a MIB view remote to it, and the receiver answers with a Response-PDU. In both, the first two variable bindings are sysUpTime.0 and snmpTrapOID.0.

The Response-PDU is only generated on receipt of a Get, GetNext, GetBulk, Set or Inform request. If its error-status is non-zero, the value fields are ignored. A Report-PDU is defined, but its use and meaning are left to the administrative framework that uses it.
sections.eli5: A trap is a device shouting that something just happened. An inform is the same news, but the listener must say thank you so the sender knows it was heard.
